checks.claim: Ancient Greek thinkers counted water as one of four elements with earth, air and fire (Empedocles' four roots, kept by Aristotle); modern chemists do not (Lavoisier 1789 demoted all four)
Key: an electric current splits water into two gases, hydrogen and oxygen (2:1 by volume; Nicholson and Carlisle, 1800), so water is a compound, not an element
An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means
Wrong choice 'A hot flame boils it away into steam' is no evidence: boiling only changes water's state; the bubbles are water vapour, not hydrogen and oxygen
Wrong choice 'A hard frost freezes it into solid ice' is no evidence: a change of state only
Wrong choice 'Salt and many minerals dissolve in it' is no evidence: salt water is a homogeneous mixture (a solution), no new substance formed
Charcoal is mostly elemental carbon, a black solid that burns; oxygen is needed for fire (fire triangle); burning carbon gives carbon dioxide
Key: carbon dioxide is a colourless gas that puts out flames (colourless, odourless, nonflammable; used in extinguishers because it displaces oxygen)
checks.note: Reactive metals such as magnesium burn in CO2 (Grokipedia notes this), but for ordinary fires the key holds at this grade.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'A colourless gas that makes flames brighter' describes oxygen, not carbon dioxide
Wrong choices 'A black smoke that catches fire easily' and 'A black powder that burns like charcoal' are false of CO2 (a colourless nonflammable gas)
Context: CO2 does not burn or feed a fire, and fire extinguishers use it to smother flames by shutting out oxygen
checks.note: Only some extinguishers are CO2 types; 'fire extinguishers use it' is acceptable as a generic statement, though 'some fire extinguishers' would be more exact.

checks.claim: Context: 'It is also the gas that every person breathes out'
checks.note: People do exhale CO2, but exhaled air is about 78% nitrogen, 16-17% oxygen and only about 4% CO2. 'THE gas that every person breathes out' feeds the common misconception that we breathe out carbon dioxide instead of oxygen. Fix: 'It is also one of the gases every person breathes out.'

checks.claim: Key: brass is a homogeneous mixture (an alloy, a solid solution of zinc in copper)
checks.note: Grokipedia's Mixture page gives 'alloys like brass (copper and zinc)' as a homogeneous solid solution. Fine point only: brasses above about 35-37% zinc (alpha-beta or duplex brass, e.g. 60/40 Muntz metal) have a two-phase microstructure, so strictly only alpha brass is a single solid solution. At grade 6 brass is the standard textbook example of a homogeneous mixture and every sample looks uniform; no change needed.

checks.claim: Context: brass's zinc share varies, generally about 5 to 40 percent
Context: brass is copper and zinc melted together
checks.note: Modern brass is made by melting the two metals together (older cementation brass heated copper with zinc ore), so the simple statement is true.

checks.claim: Wrong choice Copper: an element, so a pure substance, not a mixture
Wrong choice Distilled water: boiled and condensed water, essentially free of impurities (total dissolved solids near 0 ppm), a pure compound
Wrong choice Granite: a heterogeneous mixture of quartz, feldspar and mica whose crystals are visible to the naked eye
Key: after standing, the jar shows layers with sand at the bottom and clay on top (sand, then silt, then clay)
checks.note: Clemson: the clay layer 'has settled on top of the silt layer' after 48 hours. The writer is right that clay settles last.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'clay at the bottom and sand on top' is the reverse of the real order
Wrong choice 'Brown, muddy water, still the same all through' after three days
checks.note: Colorado State says clay typically clears in 1 to 3 days, 'some soils may take weeks'; even then the sand and silt have long settled, so the jar is never the same all through.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Clear water, with all the soil dissolved in it': sand (quartz) has negligible solubility; soil grains settle rather than dissolve
Context times: sand within a minute, silt within a couple of hours, clay over a day or more
checks.note: Both extension sheets: sand marked at 1 minute, silt at 2 hours, clay at 48 hours / 1 to 3 days.

checks.claim: Context: soil is a heterogeneous mixture; sand is the biggest grain, clay the tiniest (sand 0.05-2 mm, silt 0.002-0.05 mm, clay under 0.002 mm)
Pure water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level
Key: seawater boils a little above 100 because dissolved salt raises the boiling point
Context number: seawater boils at about 100.6 degrees Celsius
checks.note: The J E Hall property table (data from M. Hill (ed.), The Sea, Wiley) gives 'Boiling point 100.56' at salinity 35 g/kg and atmospheric pressure, and the LSBU water site is reported (search listing; the page itself would not load) to give 100.56 C for IAPSO standard seawater; 'about 100.6' is a fair rounding, and the key's 'a little above 100' needs no exact figure. Grokipedia's Seawater page gives the 35 g/kg salinity but no boiling point.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'a little below 100': salt raises, not lowers, the boiling point
Wrong choices 'at 100 too, as only its water boils away' and 'at 100 too, as dissolved salt has no effect'
checks.note: Only the water does boil off, but the nonvolatile salt still raises the boiling point, so both are wrong.

checks.claim: Context: as water boils away and the brine grows more concentrated, the boiling point climbs higher still
checks.note: Elevation is proportional to molality in dilute solutions; concentrated brines over 100 g/kg rise 3-5 C.

checks.claim: Key: the dye stays behind because it does not boil when the water does (distillation separates by boiling point)
checks.note: RSC: 'it is only water that distils off when a solution is boiled', and ink is named as the traditional coloured solution for this experiment.

checks.claim: A cold, water-cooled tube (condenser) turns the steam back into liquid water
checks.note: Oak: the condenser is 'a tube surrounded by a cold layer, usually cold water'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'The cold tube filters the dye from the steam': the condenser only cools; the vapour carries no dye
Wrong choices 'The dye sinks to the flask's bottom when hot' and 'The dye sticks fast to the flask's hot glass': the dye stays dissolved in the remaining ink because it is nonvolatile
checks.note: RSC notes the solution left in the flask darkens as it concentrates, i.e. the colour stays dissolved.

checks.claim: Context: water boils at about 100 C; the dye does not boil at that temperature
checks.note: The ink boils slightly above 100 C (boiling-point elevation); 'about' covers it. Many dyes decompose rather than boil, but 'does not boil at that temperature' stays true.

checks.claim: Key: gold stays in the pan because it is many times denser than sand (gravity separation; lighter sand and gravel washed out, gold settles)
Context numbers: gold about 19 times denser than water (19.3 g/cm3) and about seven times denser than quartz (2.65 g/cm3; 19.3 / 2.65 = 7.3)
Context: quartz is the main mineral in sand
checks.note: Often 90-95% or more of continental sands (stream sands included); marine and tropical sands can be mostly calcium carbonate, but a stream bed's sand is the quartz kind.

checks.claim: Stem: a wide steel pan dipped and swirled under water
checks.note: Steel pans were common in the early gold rushes; modern pans are mostly plastic, but steel ones are real.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Gold is magnetic and clings to the steel pan': pure gold is not magnetic (very weakly diamagnetic, slightly repelled)
Wrong choice 'Sand dissolves in water, but gold does not': quartz sand has negligible solubility in water (under 10^-5 g/L at neutral pH)
Wrong choice 'Gold is harder, so water cannot move it': gold is among the softest metals (Mohs 2.5), far softer than quartz (Mohs 7)
Key: spring water is not a pure substance because rock minerals are dissolved in it (spring water is groundwater that carries dissolved minerals)
checks.note: USGS: 'as water moves through soil and rock it dissolves small amounts of naturally-occurring minerals'.

checks.claim: Context: the dissolved minerals include calcium and magnesium
checks.note: Grokipedia: calcium, magnesium and bicarbonate in limestone and dolomite country; the mix depends on the rock.

checks.claim: Context: to a chemist a pure substance is a single element or compound, so pure water is a pure substance
Wrong choice 'No, since water is a compound, not an element' gives a false reason: a compound is a pure substance
checks.note: Right verdict, wrong reason; the stem asks for the chemist's view and the reason is part of each choice, so it is truly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'Yes, since it comes straight from nature' and 'Yes, since it is clear and clean to drink' use the everyday sense of pure, not the chemist's
checks.note: Dissolved minerals make a homogeneous mixture that can be perfectly clear.

unit_notes: 8 questions: 7 ok, 1 uncertain, 0 errors. The flagged points all hold: seawater at 35 g/kg boils at 100.56 C (verified in the J E Hall property table, data from Hill's The Sea), so 'about 100.6' stands; electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen; CO2 is colourless and nonflammable; brass is the standard homogeneous-mixture example (fine print: duplex brass above about 37% zinc is two-phase at the microscopic scale); in the soil jar sand settles first (bottom) and clay last (top), per Clemson and Colorado State extension; distilling ink leaves the dye behind (RSC); gold panning works by density (19.3 vs 2.65 for quartz); spring water carries dissolved minerals (USGS). One wording fix suggested in ec59d633ca: 'the gas every person breathes out' should be 'one of the gases', since exhaled air is only about 4% CO2.
